title: Silence
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane offers three practical tips for running productive silent work, framed around the idea that silence only works well when the teacher's system for it is well executed, otherwise it degrades into constant bickering over norms. 'Stand and scan,' borrowed from Doug Lemov, means resisting the urge to immediately start circulating and helping individual students, and instead standing where the whole class is visible until everyone has genuinely started. 'Golden silence,' from Adam Boxer, extends that further: waiting not just for quiet but for a durable, library-like silence where a student can get up for a tissue without triggering a cascade of whispers, since circulating too early re-triggers conversation. The third tip, '4-2' from Craig Barton, structures a task into four minutes of silent work followed by two minutes of partner discussion, which Kane finds makes tasks feel more manageable via a visible timer, produces more focused partner talk since he can target discussion at problems students actually struggled with, and flexes easily (he adjusts to 4-1 for a chattier class). Kane closes by noting that as he's gotten better at executing these systems, he finds himself defaulting to silent work more often, not because he has a fixed philosophy about the ideal ratio of silent to social work, but because well-run silence produces more actual math thinking with less time spent managing the class.
points: Kane's 'stand and scan' tip (from Doug Lemov) argues the biggest threat to a good silent-work routine is the teacher's own instinct to immediately start circulating and helping individuals, which undercuts the accountability moment.

'Golden silence' (from Adam Boxer) extends the standard beyond mere quiet to a durable, library-like silence, arguing that circulating even slightly too early re-triggers whispering and undoes the routine.

The '4-2' structure (from Craig Barton) pairs four minutes of silent work with two minutes of targeted partner talk, and Kane reports adapting the ratio (to 4-1) for a chattier class, showing the routine's built-in flexibility.

Kane's closing observation, that he finds himself using silent work more as his execution improves, reframes the debate over ideal ratios of silent-to-social work as secondary to whether the system is actually well run.
quotes: I don't know that I have very strong opinions about the right proportion of silent work, partner work, or any other type.
The most important thing I've learned about silent work is that I need to execute my system for silent work well.
When I ask students to begin a chunk of silent work, the first thing I do is stand somewhere I can see every student and scan the room.
Golden silence is durable. It's the silence you feel when you walk into a library, and without even thinking about it you know you don't want to bother anyone.
4 - 2 is a routine where students work quietly for 4 minutes, then do 2 minutes of partner work discussing their answers.
As I've gotten better at facilitating silent work, as I spend less time bickering with students and students spend more of the time doing math, I find myself using silence more often.
